claims.text: The baseline material is a refractory HEA such as NbMoTaW.
The baseline is fabricated by vacuum arc melting followed by homogenization and controlled thermomechanical processing.
The baseline has a coarse-grained, oxide-free microstructure.
The intervention adds approximately 1–2 wt.% Y2O3 to the refractory HEA.
High-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering or hot isostatic pressing can produce a uniform nanoscale Y2O3 dispersion in the alloy matrix.
The resulting structural mediator is a stable, uniform nanoscale dispersion of Y2O3 particles both at grain boundaries and within grains.
The dispersed oxide particles impede dislocation motion through dispersion or precipitation strengthening.
The dispersed oxide particles restrict grain growth.
Dislocation impediment and grain-growth restriction increase the alloy's strength.
The refractory nature and chemical stability of Y2O3 help preserve the thermal stability of the HEA.
The oxide dispersion helps preserve irradiation stability by preventing radiation-induced segregation.
The oxide dispersion helps preserve irradiation stability by preventing detrimental coarsening.
Adding 1–2 wt.% Y2O3 will increase yield strength relative to the oxide-free baseline.
Adding 1–2 wt.% Y2O3 will increase hardness relative to the oxide-free baseline.
The Y2O3-dispersed alloy will retain thermal stability comparable to that of the oxide-free baseline.
The Y2O3-dispersed alloy will retain irradiation resistance comparable to that of the oxide-free baseline.
The proposed benefits should hold during high-temperature operation up to approximately 1000°C and under irradiation exposure.
The beneficial effects require an oxide content of approximately 1–2 wt.% and processing that produces a uniform nanoscale dispersion.
Excessive oxide content or an inhomogeneous dispersion may cause embrittlement.
Excessive oxide content or an inhomogeneous dispersion may degrade thermal or irradiation stability.
